full_judgment: 35. In this case, thus, it is evident that the respondent-company is not willing to pay. If a debtor is merely unwilling to pay his debts, then the usual course of seeking remedy should be a suit, inasmuch as a suit is the straightforward course for proving one's claim directly and then executing the Decree. And, if his debt is undisputed, the Decree shall follow easily. When a creditor files an application for winding up of a company for recovery of a disputed debt, instead of instituting a suit against the debtor-company, he should ask himself why he is doing so. If he simply intends to escape the Court-fees, then, the consideration of paying less to the State revenue might ultimately be turned out to be a wrong option when he would find it difficult to prove insolvency of the company, for, 'commercial insolvency' is different from a 'temporary misfortune of a company'. And, when there is not even 'temporary misfortune of a company', not to speak of 'commercial insolvency', which has been the scenario of the instant case following its scrutinization, the winding up application is bound to fail. Therefore, it is always a better course to seek to have a Decree for a disputed debt and, thereafter, get it executed by the civil Court. After succeeding in civil suit, thus, the Decree-holder should not opt for executing the same through filing winding up application. Because, the said route may not be an easier one inasmuch as even after passing a Decree by a competent civil Court, the existence of a bona fide dispute is applicable to a decretal debt as well and capable of dispelling the fiction or presumption contained in section 242 of the Companies Act. The only difference is that the Decree against the alleged debtor raises a strong presumption that a genuine debt exists. The presumption can, however, be rebutted where there are substantial grounds for questioning the validity of the Decree. But, a debt simpliciter, which is not supported by a Judgment as evidence, has to be proved by other evidence. The difference lies not in the principle applicable but in the type of evidence produced to prove a debt and its effect. While this Court is of the view that a winding-up order may be a form of equitable execution, there is no equity in making such an order when the debt of the creditor is not in peril, although the substratum of the company may be gone, and when matters remain outstanding which can be best attended to in the interest of the share-holders by the company functioning as a company through its directors. It is trite law that a winding-up order is not a normal alternative in the case of a company to, the ordinary procedure for the realisation of debts due from it.
